title: Hun-Medipharma (Jan 1999 TCC) Tax Court Canada Case
subject: TCC informal-procedure appeal assessing whether pharmaceutical research without formal clinical trials qualified as SR&ED.
outcome: Appeal allowed; court held systematic experimental drug research qualified even without formal clinical trials.
summary: Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen (99 DTC 407, TCC, 1999) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian corporations claiming research credits under the Income Tax Act. The Court allowed the taxpayer's appeal for its 1994 taxation year, holding that a systematic investigation may qualify by means of analysis alone, without clinical experiments.
metaDescription: Explore the January 1999 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Hun-Medipharma and its lessons for Canadian R&D tax claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural History and Corporate Context

On January 22, 1999, Judge Louise Lamarre Proulx of the Tax Court of Canada signed the reasons for judgment in Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, Docket 97-2305(IT)I (recorded in the Court's judgment database under the date of January 28, 1999, following a hearing held at Montréal, Quebec, on January 12, 1999), reported at 99 DTC 407 (TCC). Heard under the Informal Procedure of the Tax Court of Canada pursuant to the Tax Court of Canada Act, the appeal involved Hun-Medipharma Research Inc., a Canadian corporation incorporated on March 3, 1982, and operating within the pharmaceutical research and manufacturing corridor at 53 Rue Grace-Shantz in Kirkland, Quebec.

The dispute arose after the Minister of National Revenue, then administering the federal Income Tax Act through Revenue Canada (now the Canada Revenue Agency, or CRA), assessed the appellant to disallow part of its claimed Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) for its 1994 taxation year, the only taxation year under appeal. The appellant had claimed only salaries as SR&ED expenditures; the Minister refused $8,357 of wages and salaries ($5,014 net of the consequently adjusted Quebec tax credit of $3,343), refused a consequential prescribed proxy amount of $151, and reduced the allowable ITC by $1,808 (35% of $5,165). Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. filed a Notice of Objection to the assessment of Part I tax payable and subsequently appealed to the Tax Court of Canada, contending that its pharmaceutical and biomedical research activities satisfied the statutory definition of SR&ED, thereby entitling the corporation to deduct its current SR&ED expenditures (consisting solely of salaries) under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), as amended, hereinafter the "ITA") and to claim ITCs under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA.

The reasons for judgment do not cite or apply the judicial framework established by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC); instead, Hun-Medipharma turns on the text of subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations and stands for the proposition that a systematic investigation carried out in a field of science may be made by means of analysis alone, without clinical or laboratory experiments, where it is undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.
Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

The statutory architecture governing the dispute in Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen is anchored in three interlocking regimes within the federal Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "Regulations"). Prior to the 1995–1996 legislative amendments, the substantive definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was located in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations. Parliament subsequently migrated the definition into subsection 248(1) of the ITA in revised form; because the appeal concerned the 1994 taxation year, the Court applied subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations, which defined SR&ED as systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, namely (a) basic research, (b) applied research, and (c) development, namely, use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, and which excluded, among other things, market research or sales promotion, quality control or routine testing, research in the social sciences or the humanities, commercial production, style changes and routine data collection. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". This statutory definition encompasses three core categories of research alongside a restricted category of eligible support work. Paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c) covers experimental development, which comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

In addition to core research, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly carve out and exclude routine commercial and technical activities from SR&ED eligibility, including market research or sales promotion, quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes, research in the social sciences or the humanities, prospecting, exploring or drilling for minerals, petroleum or natural gas, the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process, style changes, and routine data collection.

The second statutory pillar is section 37 of the ITA, which governs the pooling and deductibility of SR&ED expenditures. Subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature (and, prior to the 2014 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility, expenditures of a capital nature) made in Canada on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Crucially, paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool be reduced by the amount of any government assistance or non-government assistance (as those terms are defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of SR&ED expenditures that, at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive. Furthermore, subsection 37(8) establishes the rules for electing either the Traditional Method (claiming specifically identified overhead expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED) or the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method, under which overhead is calculated as a notional percentage of the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada.

The third statutory pillar comprises sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, which govern the generation and refundability of Investment Tax Credits. Subsection 127(5) permits a deduction from Part I tax otherwise payable in respect of a taxpayer's "investment tax credit" at the end of a taxation year, defined in subsection 127(9) to include a specified percentage of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" incurred in the year on SR&ED. For a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) that satisfies the statutory taxable income and taxable capital thresholds, section 127.1 provides for the refundability of the enhanced 35% ITC rate up to the corporation's expenditure limit, whereas basic ITCs are earned at the general statutory rate (20% during the 1994 taxation year under appeal, subsequently reduced to 15%).
The Minister's Challenge and the Final Holding of the Tax Court

In Hun-Medipharma, the Minister of National Revenue, relying on the conclusion of the Revenue Canada scientist advisor that part of the projects did not qualify as SR&ED projects, challenged the scientific eligibility of part of the appellant's claimed work. Although the taxpayer generally bears the onus of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact pleaded in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal, the Court found it doubtful that the Reply conformed with paragraph 6(1) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (Informal Procedure), because it was not possible from its reading to determine the findings or assumptions of fact made by the Minister, and it was not sufficient to say only that the Minister's scientist advisor had refused the claim. The scientist advisor's eligibility report concluded that the only activity in Project 1/b in 1994 was the preparation of a drug identification number (DIN) application submitted to the Health Protection Branch of Health Canada on February 11, 1994, which alone is not an eligible activity; she testified that the work consisted only of a review of the literature in preparation for that application, without clinical trials, made the same comments about the skin care project while acknowledging that conceptual work had been done on it, and stated that she did not doubt the appellant's credentials. Furthermore, counsel for the Respondent, relying on Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363, argued that a systematic investigation would certainly require some form of clinical experiments and that the appellant had completed no such experiments during the relevant period; the Court also noted that the appellant itself had changed its view of the exact nature of the work between the filing of its Form T661 claim and the review of the claim at the appeals level.

The Tax Court of Canada allowed the taxpayer's appeal, without costs. Evaluating the evidence placed before the bench, including the testimony of Mr. Fazekas, who explained that data gathered in Germany concerning a drug used for one purpose had been analysed for the appellant's different purpose and who produced many documents to evidence that the analysis was systematic, and without citing Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839), The Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527) or RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087), the Court held that the R&D expenses claimed by the appellant appeared, on a balance of probability, to be within the meaning of subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations, because they were incurred for the systematic investigation carried out in the field of science by means of analysis for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Rejecting the Respondent's reliance on the absence of clinical experiments, the Court found that paragraph 5.1 of Information Circular 86-4R3 does not make such a requirement and, above all, that the text of subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations does not require the systematic investigation to be made by both experiment and analysis: it can be made by experiment or analysis, provided it is in fact a systematic investigation.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Issues

A forensic examination of the ruling in Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC), and its subsequent treatment in Canadian tax jurisprudence reveals five interconnected legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary issues that frame SR&ED claims; on the record before it, the Court resolved the contested eligibility issue in the taxpayer's favour.
2.1 Proving Genuine Scientific or Technological Uncertainty

Under the first criterion of the judicial test for SR&ED, a taxpayer must establish whether there was a "scientific or technological uncertainty"—defined as an uncertainty that cannot be removed by standard practice, routine engineering, or reference to publicly available scientific or technical knowledge. In the pharmaceutical and biomedical sector, a recurring legal failure occurs when taxpayers conflate commercial, regulatory, or operational uncertainty with genuine scientific or technological uncertainty.

In Hun-Medipharma, the Court made no finding that the taxpayer failed to identify a scientific or technological uncertainty; rather, it observed that the hearing would have been more purposeful had the Minister's assumptions of fact in the Reply defined what was at issue, including the technological or scientific uncertainty and the investigatory means and its value. When a pharmaceutical researcher does not know whether a specific compound, excipient blend, or dosage formulation will achieve commercial viability, pass regulatory bioequivalence thresholds, or exhibit acceptable shelf-life under standard International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) stability conditions, that lack of prior confirmation represents an empirical unknown rather than a scientific uncertainty. If the methodology required to determine the outcome relies on established analytical chemistry, standard pharmacopeial assays (such as USP dissolution testing or high-performance liquid chromatography profiling), and predictable formulation adjustment rules known to a competent professional in the field, the work constitutes "quality control or routine testing" or "routine data collection" excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) of the ITA. The Tax Court emphasized that the Respondent's Reply should have specifically identified the technological or scientific uncertainty, the investigatory means and its value, or the other pertinent points as to why the R&D expenses were disallowed, rather than merely stating that the Minister's scientist advisor had refused the claim.
2.2 Structured, Systematic Process of Experimentation or Analysis

The second and third judicial criteria mandate that the taxpayer formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty, and that the overall approach adopted be consistent with the scientific method—characterized as a "systematic investigation or search ... by means of experiment or analysis" under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

In Hun-Medipharma, the Respondent relied on Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363, in which the Tax Court stated that systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and highly accurate measurements and involves the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence; the Court in Hun-Medipharma nonetheless held that experimentation is not mandatory, because a systematic investigation may be made by experiment or analysis. Where an investigation proceeds by experiment, Canadian SR&ED practice typically looks for a rigorous four-stage iterative cycle. This cycle begins with the observation of the governing scientific principles and explicit definition of the limiting technical boundary, followed by the formulation of a testable, falsifiable hypothesis explaining why a specific manipulation of independent variables is predicted to resolve the bottleneck. The researcher must then execute controlled experiments or mathematical and chemical analyses governed by predefined test protocols, and subsequently collect test data and test results, culminating in a rigorous analysis of test results that logically informs the next experimental iteration or confirms the hypothesis.

In Hun-Medipharma, however, the Court did not require proof of such an experimental cycle, because the claimed work was a scientific and medical analysis of available published and unpublished technical, preclinical and clinical data aimed at identifying a first medical-clinical indication. Mr. Fazekas produced many documents to evidence the fact that the analysis was systematic, and the Court accepted, on a balance of probability, that the work was a systematic investigation carried out by means of analysis.
2.3 Contemporaneous Documentation and Post-Hoc Reconstruction

Documentation was not the decisive issue in Hun-Medipharma: the appellant's president produced many documents to evidence that the analysis was systematic, the scientist advisor's report referred to the company's log book recording 13 to 14 days of activities, and the Court did not disallow any expenditure for want of contemporaneous records. In Canadian SR&ED litigation, while the Income Tax Act does not prescribe a rigid statutory format for laboratory notebooks, the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839), whose criteria were endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087), included among its criteria whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed; Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407) did not address or apply that criterion.

Specifically, CRA administrative guidance and later jurisprudence, rather than Hun-Medipharma itself, articulate two evidentiary propositions. First, although a taxpayer is not required to submit all underlying raw experimental evidence with the initial Form T661 claim filing, all records and other evidence must be generated contemporaneously and kept so that they can be produced upon audit or appeal to substantiate that eligible SR&ED was actually carried out. Second, the contemporaneous documentation must affirmatively show the work that was necessary to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties by preserving four specific, dated artifacts: test protocols, test data, test results, and the analysis of those test results.

When a taxpayer relies on high-level executive summaries, undated summary sheets, or witness testimony given years after the taxation year in question without corroborated bench logs or failure analyses, the Tax Court judge—who is tasked with evaluating the weight and credibility of the evidence placed before the Court—accords minimal evidentiary weight to self-serving oral recollections. Subsequent jurisprudence such as ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263, has also weighed oral testimony and other records where formal documentation was incomplete; Hun-Medipharma, for its part, does not stand for a strict documentation rule, since the Court allowed the claim on the basis of the president's testimony and supporting documents and held that a systematic investigation carried out by means of analysis satisfies the definition.
2.4 Establishing Scientific or Technological Advancement

Under the fourth criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the overall process must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement. In Canadian SR&ED law, technological advancement does not require a radical industry breakthrough, nor does it require the project to succeed commercially or technically; indeed, the refutation of a well-formulated hypothesis through rigorous experimentation advances technological knowledge by proving that a theoretically plausible pathway is unviable.

In Hun-Medipharma, the Court accepted that the appellant's work, an analysis for the appellant's own purpose of data gathered in Germany concerning a drug used for a different purpose, was carried out for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, and therefore constituted applied research within subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations. When a pharmaceutical firm combines known active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) with standard excipients using established wet-granulation, tableting, or lyophilization techniques, the resulting product may be new to the company's catalog or newly approved for sale by Health Canada, but the underlying technological state of the art remains unchanged. To prove technological advancement, a taxpayer generally must establish the baseline of standard practice available to a competent professional at the outset of the taxation year and demonstrate how the systematic investigation sought to generate new scientific principles or extend technological capabilities beyond that established baseline.
2.5 Contractual, Financial, and Expenditure Allocation Considerations

Beyond the scientific eligibility criteria of subsection 248(1), SR&ED claims may encounter compounding disqualifications under the financial and contractual rules of sections 37, 127, and 230 of the ITA, although in Hun-Medipharma itself the appellant claimed only salaries and the dispute concerned the eligibility of the work rather than expenditure allocation, contracts or third-party funding. Even where fragments of experimental work occur, a taxpayer must prove under subsection 37(1) that the claimed salaries and wages (under either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method elected under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), materials consumed or transformed, and subcontractor fees were incurred directly in the prosecution of eligible SR&ED in Canada or on work "directly in support" of SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(d). As illustrated by contemporaneous Tax Court jurisprudence such as LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 675 (TCC), proving that peripheral or off-site activities constitute an essential, directly supporting part of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada requires rigorous factual substantiation. Where personnel divide hours between commercial production, regulatory compliance, corporate administration, and laboratory research without contemporaneous project-level time tracking, the Minister is entitled to disallow uncorroborated salary allocations.

Furthermore, subcontractor and contract payment ambiguities under paragraph 37(1)(a), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsection 127(9) create severe exposure when pharmaceutical companies engage external laboratories, universities, or Contract Research Organizations (CROs) to perform bio-analytical assays or stability runs. To qualify as an eligible SR&ED contract expenditure, the written agreement must establish that the work was performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer in Canada, that the taxpayer retained the technological risk and intellectual property rights, and that the statement of work mapped directly to paragraph 248(1)(d) support activities commensurate with the needs of the taxpayer's core SR&ED project. Conversely, if the taxpayer performs research funded by an affiliate, commercial partner, or public authority, any "contract payment" or "government or non-government assistance" must be taken into account: assistance reduces the SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d), and both assistance and contract payments reduce qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20), preventing the duplication of tax credits across Canadian taxpayers.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement governing Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC), against the taxpayer's position and the Court's findings in that case, and the corresponding evidentiary benchmarks applied in Canadian SR&ED practice.

headers: Taxpayer's Position and Court's Finding in Hun-Medipharma
Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Benchmark in Canadian SR&ED Practice

cells: 1. Existence of Scientific or Technological Uncertainty
ITA s. 248(1) (formerly Reg. 2900(1)); Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839); Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407)
Not found deficient: the Court made no finding that the taxpayer failed to establish an uncertainty, and criticized the Reply for not defining the technological or scientific uncertainty at issue.

The taxpayer must establish, through objective baseline evidence (literature reviews, patent searches, expert testimony), a fundamental system constraint or gap in scientific knowledge that a competent professional in the field could not resolve using publicly available knowledge or routine engineering/formulation.
2. Formulation of Specific Scientific Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search"); Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407)

Not at issue: the Court did not require formal hypotheses; the claimed work was a systematic analysis of published and unpublished technical, preclinical and clinical data to identify a first medical-clinical indication.

The taxpayer must produce dated, pre-experimental records articulating a causal proposition linking specific independent variables to predicted technical outcomes, specifically designed to reduce or eliminate the defined technological uncertainty.
3. Execution of a Systematic Investigation by Experiment or Analysis
ITA s. 248(1); RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087); Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407)
Accepted: the Court held that a systematic investigation was carried out by means of analysis and that clinical experiments were not required.

Where the investigation proceeds by experiment, evidence typically demonstrates adherence to the scientific method through a closed-loop cycle (under Hun-Medipharma, an investigation by analysis alone may also qualify): (i) formal test protocols, (ii) recorded test data, (iii) objective test results, and (iv) documented analysis of test results driving subsequent experimental iterations.
4. Pursuit of Scientific or Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(a)–(c); Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839); Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407)
Accepted: the Court found the work was undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (applied research).

The taxpayer must prove that the investigation generated (or systematically attempted to generate) new scientific knowledge or technological understanding that advances the general stock of knowledge beyond standard industry practice, regardless of commercial success.
5. Retention of Contemporaneous Documentation
ITA s. 230(1), s. 248(1); RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087); Hun-Medipharma (99 DTC 407)
Not found deficient: the president produced many documents evidencing the systematic analysis, the company kept a log book of activities, and no expenditure was disallowed for lack of records.

While supporting records need not be filed with the initial T661 return, all records and evidence must be generated contemporaneously and retained. The documentation must contemporaneously show the exact work necessary to overcome the uncertainty, including raw data and failure analyses.
6. Eligibility of Support Work & Exclusion of Routine Testing
ITA s. 248(1)(d) and (e)–(k); LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 675)

Not at issue: the dispute concerned the analysis of data and the preparation of a DIN application (which the scientist advisor considered ineligible on its own, and for which the appellant stated at the hearing that it had claimed no expenditures), not stability testing or support work.

Testing, data collection, and analysis under para. 248(1)(d) are eligible only if they directly serve to test a hypothesis within an eligible basic, applied, or experimental development project; standalone commercial validation or quality control is strictly excluded under para. 248(1)(f).
7. Substantiation of Qualified Expenditures & Contractual Rights
ITA s. 37(1), s. 37(8), s. 127(5), s. 127(9)

Not at issue: the appellant claimed only salaries; the amount in dispute was $8,357 of wages and salaries (with a consequential $151 prescribed proxy amount and a $1,808 ITC reduction), and no third-party testing or funding arrangements were in question.

The taxpayer bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities through contemporaneous time sheets, general ledger cost centers, and explicit written contracts that every dollar claimed was incurred directly on eligible SR&ED performed on its behalf in Canada, net of any assistance or contract payments.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC), into actionable tax compliance and risk-mitigation protocols, the following two applied case studies examine realistic Canadian corporate research initiatives that initially exhibit legal, technical, and evidentiary vulnerabilities commonly challenged by the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada under the Northwest Hydraulic criteria (in Hun-Medipharma itself, the Court allowed the taxpayer's appeal). For each scenario, a comprehensive four-pillar remediation architecture is detailed in narrative form.
4.1 Case Study 1: Specialty Pharmaceutical Formulation & Sustained-Release Delivery Matrix (Quebec Life Sciences Sector)
Corporate Profile and Project Scenario

KinetiPharm BioSciences Inc. ("KinetiPharm") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Kirkland, Quebec, operating a pharmaceutical formulation and drug delivery laboratory in the same life sciences corridor as the appellant in Hun-Medipharma. During its fiscal year ended December 31, KinetiPharm undertook a project titled Development of a Transdermal Liposomal Hydrogel for Sustained 72-Hour Delivery of a Hydrophobic Analgesic API (Project TLH-72).

The commercial objective of Project TLH-72 was to formulate a topical patch capable of delivering a steady-state plasma concentration of a poorly water-soluble active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) over 72 hours without inducing skin irritation or drug crystal precipitation. During the taxation year, KinetiPharm prepared 48 distinct hydrogel formulation batches, conducted Franz diffusion cell permeation assays, and contracted a Montreal-based Contract Research Organization (CRO), BioAssay Quebec Inc., to perform high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) stability and purity testing. On its federal return, KinetiPharm claimed $920,000 in qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661, electing the Proxy Method for overhead calculations under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA, and claimed refundable federal ITCs at the 35% CCPC enhanced rate under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and section 127.1, alongside Quebec R&D tax credits (crédit d'impôt pour la recherche scientifique et le développement expérimental) under the Taxation Act (Quebec).
Vulnerability Diagnostic: How KinetiPharm Triggers the Hun-Medipharma Pitfalls

Under a joint review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer, KinetiPharm's initial claim posture is highly vulnerable to complete disallowance under the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and CRA documentation policy, notwithstanding that Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen was decided in the taxpayer's favour. First, KinetiPharm conflated formulation screening with technological uncertainty: on Form T661 (Part 2, Line 242), the corporation described its uncertainty as whether a stable 72-hour transdermal hydrogel patch meeting Health Canada bioequivalence standards could be formulated at commercial scale. As the dispute in Hun-Medipharma illustrates, where the Revenue Canada scientist advisor regarded the preparation of a DIN application, on its own, as not an eligible activity, this phrasing describes a commercial and regulatory objective rather than an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty. Second, the laboratory engaged in unstructured trial-and-error batching. KinetiPharm's laboratory records consisted merely of 48 manufacturing batch sheets showing varying ratios of phospholipids, ethanol, and carbomer polymers, followed by pass/fail Franz cell flux rates. There were no written test protocols explaining the scientific rationale for changing excipient ratios between Batches 1 through 48, nor any mechanistic analysis of test results explaining why recrystallization occurred at hour 36.

Third, KinetiPharm relied on retrospective narrative reconstruction. Its external tax preparer drafted the T661 technical narrative six months after year-end based on a brief interview with the Vice President of Formulation, without cross-referencing dated bench notebooks or interim scientific reports. Finally, the claim suffered from an unqualified subcontractor agreement and unsegregated labour tracking. The Master Services Agreement with BioAssay Quebec Inc. was a generic fee-for-service analytical testing contract ("ICH Q1A Stability Testing — $140,000") that made no reference to SR&ED, paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, or hypothesis testing, while KinetiPharm's three formulation chemists allocated 90% of their annual salaries to SR&ED based on year-end management estimates rather than contemporaneous time records.
Step-by-Step Remedial Compliance Architecture
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance (Separating Commercial Envelopes from Core SR&ED)

To satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and avoid the type of eligibility challenge raised by the Minister in Hun-Medipharma, KinetiPharm must institute a formal SR&ED Stage-Gate Governance Protocol overseen by a Technical Eligibility Committee—comprising the Chief Scientific Officer, Lead Formulation Chemist, and Tax Counsel—before project execution begins. Prior to claiming any experimental work, the Lead Chemist must compile and date a Gate 0 Prior Art and Technological Baseline Dossier. This dossier archives peer-reviewed pharmaceutics literature, patent filings, and excipient manufacturer technical bulletins demonstrating that standard liposomal encapsulation of the hydrophobic API at concentrations above 2% w/w induces Ostwald ripening and bilayer rupture when cross-linked inside an ionic carbomer hydrogel matrix due to osmotic pressure gradients.

Governance protocols must strictly prohibit describing commercial or regulatory targets as uncertainties. Instead, the project charter formally defines the scientific and technological uncertainty as whether steric stabilization of deformable phosphatidylcholine bilayers can be achieved in the presence of polyacrylic acid cross-linkers without suppressing the thermodynamic chemical potential gradient (Δμ) required to sustain a steady-state transdermal flux of 15 µg/cm²/h past 36 hours, given the competing kinetic conflict between vesicle rigidity and stratum corneum partitioning. Simultaneously, KinetiPharm's enterprise resource planning (ERP) system is reconfigured into two distinct project cost centers: Cost Center 100-COM (Non-SR&ED) captures pre-project literature searches, routine raw material incoming quality control, standard ICH long-term stability runs on finalized formulations, and Health Canada regulatory dossier preparation; Cost Center 200-SRED (Eligible SR&ED) captures experimental work directly investigating the vesicle-hydrogel thermodynamic conflict and commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) analytical testing.
Step 2: Overhauling Technical Documentation (The Four-Artifact Contemporaneous Standard)

To eliminate the documentation deficiencies that commonly lead to disallowance on CRA review (an issue that was not decisive in Hun-Medipharma), KinetiPharm implements an Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) system with immutable cryptographic timestamps and mandatory workflow fields that enforce the CRA's four-part contemporaneous documentation standard. First, no formulation batch under Cost Center 200-SRED may be initiated without a locked, pre-experimental ELN Test Protocol Record. Each protocol must explicitly state the specific causal hypothesis being tested—for example, Hypothesis H2.3, which posits that incorporating 5 mol% DSPE-PEG2000 into the lipid bilayer will create a hydrated steric barrier that prevents carboxylic acid protonation-induced vesicle aggregation, maintaining a vesicle polydispersity index of ≤ 0.20 without reducing transdermal diffusivity—alongside the independent variables held constant and manipulated, and the exact analytical assay methodology.

Second, the ELN captures contemporaneous raw Test Data by automatically ingesting all raw instrument outputs—including Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) particle size distributions, Zeta potential curves, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) thermograms, and raw Franz cell receptor fluid chromatograms—directly into the digital folder tied to the specific protocol identifier. Third, the ELN records structured Test Results by comparing calculated experimental metrics against the protocol's predicted baseline and explicitly logging experimental failures, such as Result R2.3, where vesicle aggregation was successfully prevented (PDI = 0.14), but transdermal flux dropped by 42% to 8.7 µg/cm²/h at hour 24. Fourth, within 72 hours of obtaining test results, the Lead Chemist must complete a mandatory Mechanistic Analysis of Test Results Log before the next experimental protocol can be opened. For Result R2.3, this analysis documents why the hypothesis failed by applying mathematical modeling based on the Higuchi release equation and Fick's first law of diffusion:

J = D × K × ΔC / h and Q = √(D × (2C₀ − Cₛ) × Cₛ × t), where J is the steady-state transdermal flux, D the diffusion coefficient, K the vesicle-to-stratum-corneum partition coefficient, ΔC the concentration gradient across the membrane, h the diffusional path length, Q the cumulative amount of API released per unit area, C₀ the initial API loading, Cₛ the API solubility in the hydrogel matrix and t the elapsed time.

This analysis demonstrates that while PEGylation resolved steric aggregation, the hydrophilic PEG corona decreased the vesicle-to-stratum-corneum partition coefficient (K) by a factor of 3.2, creating a rate-limiting barrier at the skin interface. This documented analytical insight directly generates the subsequent iteration, Hypothesis H2.4, which investigates enzyme-cleavable ester-linked PEG-lipids, thereby establishing an unbroken, contemporaneous chain of systematic investigation.
Step 3: Re-Engineering Contract Terms (Subcontractors, IP, and Canadian Nexus)

To safeguard the eligibility of the $140,000 paid to BioAssay Quebec Inc. as a qualified Canadian subcontractor expenditure under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, KinetiPharm replaces the generic testing purchase order with a dedicated SR&ED Analytical Support Statement of Work (SOW). The SOW explicitly stipulates that BioAssay Quebec Inc. is performing non-routine HPLC-MS/MS and cryo-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) characterization on behalf of KinetiPharm within Canada at its Montreal facility. Furthermore, the contract specifies that all work performed under the SOW is strictly commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of KinetiPharm's experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA, referencing KinetiPharm's specific ELN Hypothesis IDs (H1.1 through H4.6) rather than routine ICH quality control. The agreement also confirms that KinetiPharm bears the full financial and technological risk of the testing, that all resulting intellectual property, raw chromatograms, and analytical data vest exclusively and ab initio in KinetiPharm, and that BioAssay Quebec Inc. covenants not to claim federal SR&ED ITCs or Quebec R&D tax credits on the contracted work. Finally, BioAssay Quebec Inc. is contractually obligated to issue monthly invoices itemized by KinetiPharm's Hypothesis ID and experimental batch number, explicitly excluding any standard commercial stability runs.
Step 4: Experimentation & Financial Expenditure Tracking

To ensure the financial claim withstands CRA Financial Reviewer scrutiny under section 37, section 127, and subsection 230(1) of the ITA, KinetiPharm deploys a digital time-tracking system linked directly to ELN Hypothesis IDs. Scientists record their hours daily across segregated activity categories—Direct Experimental Execution (Cost Center 200-SRED), Paragraph 248(1)(d) Data Analysis and Protocol Design (Cost Center 200-SRED), and Commercial, Regulatory, or Routine QC (Cost Center 100-COM)—with mandatory bi-weekly supervisory sign-off. Simultaneously, laboratory inventory requisitions for expensive phospholipids and APIs are tagged with specific ELN Protocol IDs. Because experimental hydrogel batches are destroyed during Franz diffusion cell testing and destructive rheological assays, KinetiPharm logs these inputs as "materials consumed" in the prosecution of SR&ED under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V). Using these contemporaneously substantiated records, KinetiPharm computes its Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the directly engaged SR&ED salary base (S), ensuring salary caps for specified employees are respected under subsection 37(9.1). The resulting Qualified Expenditure Pool (QE) is calculated as:

QE = S + (0.55 × S) + M + (0.80 × C) − A, where M is the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, C is the $140,000 paid to BioAssay Quebec Inc. and A is the Quebec R&D tax credit.

In this statutory formula, 0.80 × C reflects the 80% inclusion rate for arm's-length Canadian SR&ED contract payments under subsection 127(9), and A deducts the Quebec R&D tax credit as government assistance pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9).
4.2 Case Study 2: Automated Microfluidic Point-of-Care Bio-Assay Engineering (Ontario MedTech & Diagnostics Sector)
Corporate Profile and Project Scenario

Vanguard MicroDiagnostics Ltd. ("Vanguard") is an Ontario corporation based in Mississauga, Ontario, developing point-of-care medical diagnostic hardware and embedded firmware. During its taxation year, Vanguard executed a project titled Opto-Fluidic Cartridge and Real-Time Chemiluminescence Signal Processing Engine (Project OFC-9).

Vanguard sought to engineer a disposable lab-on-a-chip microfluidic cartridge paired with a portable optical reader capable of quantifying cardiac troponin-I from whole capillary blood within 8 minutes. During development, Vanguard encountered severe signal-to-noise degradation caused by non-specific protein adsorption on the cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) microchannel walls and micro-bubble nucleation during thermal cycling, which scattered the chemiluminescent photon emission. Simultaneously, Vanguard entered into a $300,000 Collaborative Clinical Validation and Co-Development Agreement with a major Canadian hospital network, MetroHealth Hospital System, to test prototypes and co-develop clinical workflow software. On its T661 filing, Vanguard claimed $1,450,000 in SR&ED expenditures—including 100% of its hardware engineers' and firmware developers' time and all prototype tooling costs—and did not deduct the $300,000 hospital funding from its qualified expenditure pool.
Vulnerability Diagnostic: How Vanguard Triggers the Hun-Medipharma Pitfalls

If audited by the CRA or litigated before the Tax Court of Canada, Vanguard's claim faces severe exposure under the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and CRA documentation policy (Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC), was decided in the taxpayer's favour and does not itself impose these documentation requirements). First, Vanguard failed to separate system-level commercial integration from technological uncertainty. By framing its Form T661 project around the entire commercial device development lifecycle—including industrial design, printed circuit board (PCB) layout, user interface software, and cartridge injection molding—Vanguard bundled routine product engineering and standard software development with isolated physics and signal-processing bottlenecks, obscuring the specific scientific or technological uncertainty.

Second, Vanguard lacked contemporaneous hardware and software experimental logs. Its firmware engineers used Git repositories with generic commit messages (such as "fixed optical sensor bug" or "updated filter coefficients"), while its mechanical engineers retained only the final SolidWorks computer-aided design (CAD) files for the successful cartridge geometry, having overwritten the 19 failed microchannel geometries. Under the Northwest Hydraulic record-keeping criterion and CRA documentation policy, discarding intermediate designs and failing to retain test protocols, test data, test results, and analysis of test results severely undermines the taxpayer's ability to prove a systematic investigation. Third, Vanguard violated the funded research and contract payment exclusion rules. The $300,000 received from MetroHealth Hospital System was recorded as deferred commercial revenue by Vanguard's accounting team; under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, failing to deduct a contract payment or non-government assistance received in respect of SR&ED invalidates the qualified expenditure calculation.
Step-by-Step Remedial Compliance Architecture
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance (Micro-Scoping Technological Sub-Projects)

Rather than claiming the overarching commercial product development of the diagnostic analyzer, Vanguard restructures its R&D governance to isolate only those discrete technological sub-projects where standard fluid dynamics and digital signal processing (DSP) models break down. At the governance intake stage, industrial enclosure design, power supply regulation, Bluetooth connectivity, hospital database integration, and graphical user interface (GUI) development are stripped out of the SR&ED claim and assigned to commercial engineering cost codes.

The Technical Eligibility Committee then charters two discrete SR&ED sub-projects. Sub-Project SP-1 (Microfluidic Surface Physics and Bubble Nucleation) addresses the technological uncertainty of whether passive capillary micro-vortex geometries combined with plasma-polymerized zwitterionic nanocoatings can maintain laminar Poiseuille flow (Re < 1) and suppress dissolved gas cavitation under rapid Peltier thermal ramping (5 °C/s) without inducing shear-induced hemolysis of whole capillary blood. Sub-Project SP-2 (Real-Time Stochastic Photon Deconvolution) addresses the technological uncertainty of whether a real-time adaptive Kalman-Poisson deconvolution algorithm executing on a memory-constrained ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller (512 KB SRAM) can separate transient micro-bubble Mie scattering spikes from low-flux chemiluminescent photon counts (< 500 counts/s) within a deterministic 15-millisecond interrupt window.
Step 2: Overhauling Technical Documentation (Hardware Versioning & Algorithmic Experimentation Logs)

To satisfy the CRA's evidentiary expectation that contemporaneous documentation show the exact work necessary to resolve the uncertainty through test protocols, test data, test results, and analysis of test results, Vanguard institutes a strict Engineering Experimentation and Failure Archiving Protocol. For hardware experiments under Sub-Project SP-1, engineers are prohibited from overwriting failed CAD geometries; every experimental microchannel topology is archived as a distinct, read-only revision (Geo-Rev-01 through Geo-Rev-20). Each revision is paired in the company's project management and documentation repository with a pre-test computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation parameter sheet and physical test bench protocol specifying blood hematocrit levels (30–55%), thermal ramp rates, and high-speed CMOS microscopy frame rates. Raw high-speed video files, pressure transducer logs, and quantitative hemolysis spectrophotometry absorbance readings (A₅₄₀) are preserved as Test Data and Test Results, followed by a dated engineering post-mortem Analysis of Test Results explaining why specific weir angles caused boundary-layer separation and micro-vortex trapping, mathematically linking the observed wall shear stress (τ<sub>w</sub> ≥ 150 Pa) to erythrocyte membrane rupture and justifying the geometric modifications in the subsequent revision.

Similarly, for firmware experiments under Sub-Project SP-2, code commits to the experimental branch require a standardized commit template linked to a documented Algorithmic Experiment Ticket. Each ticket records the mathematical hypothesis, the simulated and physical optical test dataset identifier, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR in dB) and CPU clock-cycle profiling results, and the analytical reason why a given filter kernel failed to converge within the 15-millisecond latency ceiling.
Step 3: Re-Engineering Contract Terms (Unbundling Collaborative Agreements and Assistance)

To prevent the $300,000 MetroHealth Hospital System agreement from contaminating the entire $1,450,000 SR&ED expenditure pool as a "contract payment" or "assistance" under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, tax counsel restructures the arrangement prior to execution into two separate, standalone legal instruments. Agreement A, titled the Commercial Clinical Workflow and Integration Contract ($300,000), explicitly scopes the $300,000 payment solely to non-SR&ED commercial deliverables, including hospital IT interface customization, nurse usability studies, and routine clinical validation of finalized commercial units. Agreement A contains an explicit covenant confirming that MetroHealth is funding only commercial deployment and clinical workflow integration, and that no portion of the $300,000 is paid in respect of, or confers any rights to, Vanguard's core opto-fluidic or algorithmic SR&ED (Sub-Projects SP-1 and SP-2). Agreement B, titled the Unfunded Clinical Sample and Anonymized Data Access Agreement ($0 Consideration), governs the provision of de-identified waste capillary blood samples for Vanguard's internal laboratory testing under Sub-Project SP-1, with Vanguard retaining 100% of the intellectual property and bearing 100% of the financial risk of its internal SR&ED. To the extent any portion of third-party funding cannot be contractually severed from an SR&ED sub-project, Vanguard's tax compliance team proactively deducts that specific amount under paragraph 37(1)(d), isolating it to the affected sub-project so that unassisted expenditures remain fully eligible for ITCs.
Step 4: Experimentation & Financial Expenditure Tracking

To substantiate all claimed expenditures on a balance of probabilities, Vanguard implements a granular project accounting and physical prototype tracking framework. Under post-2013 ITA rules, where capital expenditures no longer qualify for SR&ED, Vanguard tracks every microfluidic cartridge and optical bench component by serial number. Only the 450 disposable COC cartridges and chemical reagents physically destroyed or rendered scrap during Sub-Project SP-1 destructive testing are claimed as "materials consumed" under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), whereas reusable optical test-bench oscilloscopes and commercial validation units provided to the hospital are strictly excluded from the SR&ED claim. Finally, engineers log hours daily against task tickets tagged specifically to Sub-Project SP-1, Sub-Project SP-2, or Commercial Development. At each monthly financial close, the Controller reconciles engineering ticket hours against payroll registers, ensuring that only hours corroborated by dated test protocols and analytical logs are mapped to the Form T661 salary base.

The following table synthesizes the remedial governance, documentation, contractual, and financial tracking controls implemented across both Canadian case studies to satisfy the statutory requirements of the Income Tax Act and address the eligibility issues litigated in Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC).

body.text: 5. Authoritative Conclusion for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Hun-Medipharma Research Inc. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 407 (TCC), endures as a foundational taxpayer-favourable ruling in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, holding that a systematic investigation may be carried out by means of analysis alone. Decided during the pivotal period immediately following Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen and contemporaneous with RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen and LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, Hun-Medipharma establishes that subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations does not require a systematic investigation to be made by both experiment and analysis, so that work in a field such as pharmaceutical research may qualify through systematic analysis even without clinical experiments, provided it is in fact a systematic investigation.

To prevail before the Canada Revenue Agency at the audit or Notice of Objection stage, or before the Tax Court of Canada on appeal, Canadian corporate taxpayers and their advisors must ensure that their compliance architecture generates objective, contemporaneous proof that every claimed project was initiated to resolve a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by standard practice. Above all, while Hun-Medipharma confirms that a systematic investigation may be carried out by experiment or analysis, CRA practice expects the existence of a "systematic investigation or search" under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act to be proven through preserved, dated experimental or analytical records—specifically test protocols, raw test data, test results, and rigorous analytical evaluations—demonstrating the exact work required to pursue a scientific or technological advancement. Where project governance, technical record-keeping, contractual statements of work, and financial cost accounting are integrated prospectively around these four evidentiary pillars, Canadian taxpayers can insulate their SR&ED claims from audit disallowance and secure their statutory entitlements under sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act.
